Executive Summary

Read in README.md

SQLMesh/sqlmesh holds 211 open issues (excluding 106 open PRs) as of November 20, 2026, and Reliability accounts for half the backlog at 50.7% (107 issues)—including critical silent data-loss defects in ClickHouse table swaps (), ClickHouse quorum overwrites (), UNION BY NAME column drops (), SEED CSV type inference (), and at_least_one audit false passes (). Adoption represents 24.6% (52 primary issues) and appears as a secondary driver on 69 more (57.3% total touch rate), led by dbt Jinja/ecosystem bridges (, ), enterprise auth/naming rules (, , ), and scenario walkthrough gaps (, ).

Scalability makes up 16.1% (34 primary issues), anchored by an architectural bottleneck where non-prod plan, render, test, and format load the full repository (, , ) and pure-Python virtual-layer promotion runs in O(N²)—stalling 2,400-view BigQuery dev plans for 40–50 minutes (). Extensibility is 7.1% (15 issues)—covering SQL macros (), Ossie semantic-layer generation (), ADBC drivers (), and config hooks that avoid forking EngineAdapter (, )—while 3 issues (1.4%) are genuinely Uncategorized (, , ). Because 18 of 23 existing routing labels slice orthogonally by warehouse adapter and post-Linux-Foundation unlabeled intake hit 50.0% (79.3% since August 2026), maintainers should add a required Primary Pillar Project field, retire 4 dead/vague tags, and introduce data-correctness, core: planner-state, and ecosystem-integration.

SM SQLMesh Backlog Story 01 / Shared Triage Lens
MAINTAINER CATALOGING PLAYBOOK · SQLMesh/sqlmesh 211 open issues · 32 repository labels · 106 open PRs excluded

How Pillars & Triage Labels Can Organize 211 Open Issues

What ships in Week 1 vs. Month 2 is a team decision—not something one person or one pass should dictate. First, maintainers need a shared cataloging grammar so every open issue has both an impact lens (Strategic Pillar) and a subsystem home (Triage Label).

Open Issue Scopestate:open

211

All open GitHub issues (#1391–#6228), audited end-to-end with zero sampling (194 High, 9 Medium, 8 Low confidence on sparse bodies).

Unrouted by Subsystem152 / 211

72.0%

Carry zero triage routing labels (Engine:*, Project:*, Table Format:*, Documentation), leaving core Python issues in a flat pile.

Post-LF Unlabeled SurgeSince 2026-03-25

17.3% → 50.0%

Issues with zero labels of any kind (60 / 211 overall) nearly tripled after the March 25, 2026 Linux Foundation transfer (36 / 72).

Axis 1: Strategic Pillar = Why It MattersImpact Lens

Captures the user or system contract at stake: broken behavior (Reliability), growth cost (Scalability), migration & enterprise onboarding friction (Adoption), or non-forking pluggability (Extensibility).

Axis 2: Triage Label = Where It RoutesSubsystem Lens

Routes an issue to the codebase surface and maintainers who know that subsystem: warehouse adapters (Engine:*), UI/IDE (area:*), planner/evaluator (core: planner-state), or silent data risk (data-correctness).

Welcome everyone. As we sit down together as maintainers to digest the open issue backlog, the goal of this deck is deliberately not to hand down a Week-1 or Month-1 roadmap. Prioritization is a collective call that depends on maintainer bandwidth, upcoming releases, and consensus.

What we can solve right now is how we see and organize the 211 open issues in SQLMesh/sqlmesh. Today, 72 percent of open issues lack any subsystem routing label, and since the Linux Foundation transition in March 2026, half of new open issues have zero labels at all. Over the next eight slides, we will walk through how pairing Strategic Pillars with Triage Labels turns that flat list into structured, navigable slices.

ORTHOGONAL AXES 137 of 211 issues (64.9%) span two pillars · 152 (72.0%) lack routing labels

Primary Pillar Measures Contract Health—Secondary & Labels Show Context

Our rubric assigns any crash, race, or silent wrong output to Primary: Reliability even when triggered during a dbt migration or 2,400-model plan. That is why 57 of 107 Reliability issues (53.3%) also carry Adoption (38) or Scalability (19) as secondary—so 50.7% is never a headcount split.

Primary × Secondary Pillar Cross-CutClick segment to filter

Current Triage Label Coverage by PillarBlue=Engine · Green=Surface · Red=Gap

Engine/Format: 38 (18.0%) Surface/Project: 21 (10.0%) Unrouted gap: 152 (72.0%)

Look at the two charts side by side—they explain why neither a single pillar tag nor today's GitHub labels can work alone.

On the left, Reliability is primary on 107 issues, or 50.7 percent. Why? Because our deterministic rule says whenever a supported feature crashes, regresses, or silently corrupts data, Reliability wins primary. A crash in the dbt converter gets Reliability primary and Adoption secondary—38 issues sit in that exact intersection, and another 19 sit in Reliability plus Scalability. So 50.7 percent tells us where contracts are breaking, not how to divide engineering teams.

On the right, notice the red bars: unrouted issues represent 68 percent of Reliability, 71 percent of Adoption, 76 percent of Scalability, and 93 percent of Extensibility. Clicking any bar segment jumps straight to those rows in the catalog.

PILLAR 1 · RELIABILITY 107 primary (50.7%) + 17 secondary = 124 total touch · 73/107 (68.2%) lack routing labels

Pairing Reliability with Labels Separates Adapter Bugs from Silent Data Risk

Today Bug (50 in Reliability) mixes minor UI glitches with silent data loss, while 17 broken contracts sit under Improvement. Combining Reliability with subsystem and risk labels creates three clear triage buckets:

1. Engine:* & area:*34 routed today

What belongs here: Dialect DDL, type-mapping, UI, or LSP failures isolated to one warehouse or editor surface.

  • Already routed (24 Engine, 10 Surface): Redshift DISTKEY ALTER (), UI %Title Case crash (), Project: dbt loader crashes (, ).
  • Needs dual Engine: Clickhouse + data-correctness: Swallowed _exchange_tables error () & insert_quorum="auto" override ()—both have 0 labels today.

2. + data-correctnessProposed Risk Tag

What belongs here: Silent wrong rows, dropped columns, history overwrites, or false-passing audits where plan/run exits green.

  • Schema & type loss: UNION BY NAME silent column drop ( — spans columns_to_types & sqlglot >= 30.17) and SEED CSV pre-inference (, tagged Improvement).
  • Audit & SCD2 history: 0-row at_least_one false pass () and SCD Type 2 COALESCE/truncate history loss (, , ).

3. + core: planner-stateProposed Subsystem

What belongs here: Cross-engine snapshot state, concurrency locks, model parser/loader, and interval scheduling regressions.

  • State & thread races: Concurrent plan duplicate rows () and ThreadPoolExecutor virtual-layer promotion race ().
  • Loader & cron regressions: DIALECT_PATTERN O(2^n) comment backtracking hang (), fork() segfault (), and maiden-plan cron regression (, tagged Feature + Improvement).

Let's look at how Pillars and Triage Labels work together inside Reliability. With 107 primary issues, "Reliability" on its own is still too big for a maintainer to scan.

When we cross Reliability with subsystem and risk labels, three clean buckets emerge. Bucket 1 uses our existing Engine:* and surface labels to isolate warehouse-specific and IDE bugs—and shows where dual labeling helps, like tagging ClickHouse tickets #6087 and #6171 with both Engine: Clickhouse and data-correctness.

Bucket 2 is why we propose data-correctness: tickets like #6212, #6135, #6198, and the SCD Type 2 history issues succeed green while corrupting tables, and several aren't even labeled Bug. Bucket 3 routes engine-agnostic races, regex hangs like #6203, and planner regressions like #5629 to core maintainers via core: planner-state.

PILLAR 2 · SCALABILITY 34 primary (16.1%) + 31 secondary = 65 total touch · 26/34 (76.5%) lack routing labels

Why 76.5% of Scalability Issues Are Unrouted—and How Labels Split the Work

GitHub has 13 Engine:* labels for SQL warehouses, but zero labels for SQLMesh's Python DAG loader, snapshot evaluator, or multi-hundred-model config. Crossing Scalability with labels separates three very different engineering shapes:

1. Scalability × core: planner-statePython Engine

Organizes core Python complexity—letting maintainers distinguish localized evaluator hotspots from multi-command loader architecture:

  • Promotion & render caches: O(N²) virtual-layer stall (40–50 min for ~2,400 BigQuery views in ) alongside localized cache tickets (to_table_mapping) & (snapshot_by_name).
  • Subgraph-scoped loading: Avoiding full-repo Context load on dev plan (), single-model render (), and pre-commit test/format (, ).

2. Scalability × Engine:*Warehouse I/O

Organizes SQL & storage pushdown where the bottleneck lives in adapter batching, table scans, or partition DDL rather than Python:

  • Bulk ingestion throughput: Postgres COPY protocol vs. 2–6K row/s batched VALUES inserts ().
  • Zero-scan partition ops & sampling: BigQuery copy_partitions API () and TABLESAMPLE support across 1,000-table TB warehouses ().

3. Scalability + Adoption Sec.18 Fleet UX Issues

Organizes monorepo & CI governance when boilerplate or PR blast radius scales poorly across large analytics teams:

  • Hierarchical config (O(1) repo rules): Folder-level model_defaults inheritance (), global grants (), and multi-model blueprints ().
  • CI/CD & lineage review at scale: Project: CICD Bot --select-model scoping () and OSS column-level diff summary in plan ().

Scalability is a textbook example of why current GitHub labels leave maintainers flying blind: 26 out of 34 primary Scalability issues have zero routing labels because we have labels for SQL engines, but nothing for SQLMesh's own Python graph engine.

Adding core: planner-state immediately clusters the Python DAG and promotion bottlenecks in Card 1—so maintainers discussing performance can look at localized caching tickets like #6018 and #6019 under the 2,400-view #6014 profile alongside broader subgraph-loading proposals like #5906 and #6024, without mixing them up with warehouse-specific pushdowns in Card 2 like Postgres COPY (#5830) or BigQuery copy_partitions (#5655).

And Card 3 shows the power of the Secondary Pillar: filtering Scalability primary plus Adoption secondary isolates 18 monorepo governance issues like folder-scoped model_defaults (#4996).

PILLAR 3 · ADOPTION 52 primary (24.6%) + 69 secondary = 121 total touch (57.3%) · 37/52 (71.2%) unrouted

Adoption Touches 57.3% of the Queue—Labels Split It Into 3 Maintainer Streams

Adoption spans everything from dbt parity to cloud IAM and error messages. Pairing Adoption with Project: dbt, Engine:*, Documentation, and ecosystem-integration prevents disparate onboarding blockers from blurring together:

1. Project: dbt & EcosystemMigration Stream

Separates converter bugs from missing migration bridges across the dbt ecosystem:

  • Ecosystem artifact parity (ecosystem-integration): Exporting dbt-compatible manifest.json () so elementary, BI catalogs, and governance tools keep working post-switch.
  • Package & cutover onboarding (Project: dbt + Documentation): dbt_expectations whitespace control -%} () and zero-reprocessing cutover walkthroughs ().

2. Adoption × Engine:*Enterprise & Dialect

Routes cloud security, IAM, and warehouse governance directly to dialect maintainers (8 routed today, more currently unlabeled):

  • Passwordless & long-running auth: Azure SQL Entra ID (Engine: SQL Server ) and Databricks OAuth M2M auto-refresh past 1 hour (Engine: Databricks ).
  • Enterprise deployment rules: 2-part MSSQL view names for SqlPackage DACPACs () and dialect DDL parity across ClickHouse, DuckDB, and Redshift.

3. Documentation, area:* & CLIDay-2 Ergonomics

Clusters authoring friction, error diagnostics, and docs so contributors looking for UX or docs improvements can self-serve:

  • Debuggable CLI output: Including the failing model name on warehouse driver exceptions () and [Running] start logs before multi-hour batches ().
  • Syntax & docs (Documentation [5]): Escaping @@ macro collisions with Postgres JSONPath / Snowflake stage vars (, ) & filling docs gaps (, ).

Adoption is the connective tissue of the backlog: 52 primary issues plus 69 secondary issues means 57.3 percent of open tickets touch user onboarding, migration, or day-to-day ergonomics. Yet 37 of the 52 primary Adoption tickets have zero routing labels today.

Notice how clean Adoption becomes once we cross it with labels. Stream 1 pairs Adoption with Project: dbt and our proposed ecosystem-integration label to group migration bridges like manifest.json export (#5821) separately from converter crashes. Stream 2 pairs Adoption with Engine:* so dialect maintainers can spot enterprise IAM and DACPAC blockers like #5066, #5183, and #4741. Stream 3 groups CLI diagnostics and Documentation tickets—which are also great entry points for new community contributors.

PILLAR 4 · EXTENSIBILITY 15 primary (7.1%) + 20 secondary = 35 total touch · 14/15 (93.3%) lack routing labels

93.3% of Extensibility Issues Have Zero Routing Labels—Hiding Fork Pressure

Only 1 of 15 primary Extensibility issues carries a triage label today ( Engine: Snowflake). Pairing Extensibility with core: planner-state and ecosystem-integration surfaces three architectural seams where platform teams otherwise fork SQLMesh:

1. Adapter & State SeamsStop Subclass Forks

Extensibility × core: planner-state / Engine:*: Config hooks & pluggable drivers so platform teams stop maintaining private EngineAdapter forks:

  • Configurable state & schema DDL: Snowflake Hybrid Tables for state () and create_schemas: false where DBAs lock down DDL ().
  • Bring-your-own driver & dialects: Arrow ADBC driver interface () and OracleEngineAdapter ().

2. Authoring & Runtime HooksPlugin Interfaces

Extensibility × core: planner-state: Exposing compile-time and run-time lifecycle events cleanly to user code:

  • Macro & template context: Pure-SQL MACRO definitions alongside .py () and upstream physical-table names in @resolve_template ().
  • Observer & offline hooks: NotificationTarget audit pass events () and credential-free offline sqlmesh render ().

3. External Metadata Contractsecosystem-integration

Extensibility × ecosystem-integration: Machine-readable lineage and catalog exports for external data-platform tooling:

  • Governance & semantic layers: Open Metadata Catalog connector () and Ossie semantic-layer spec generation ().
  • Portable lineage artifacts: Static HTML data catalog export from sqlmesh ui () for CI artifact hosting without a live server.

Extensibility is our smallest primary pillar at 15 issues—plus 20 more as secondary—but it has the highest label blind spot in the entire repository: 14 of those 15 issues have zero triage routing labels, so they vanish into generic Feature or Improvement lists.

Yet these tickets come from SQLMesh's most invested production adopters—teams hitting locked-down enterprise DBAs in #5623, maintaining private SnowflakeEngineAdapter forks in #5600, or wiring SQLMesh into OpenMetadata (#3565) and semantic layers (#5997). Pairing Extensibility with core: planner-state and ecosystem-integration lets core architects review interface design tickets together instead of discovering them piecemeal.

32-LABEL AUDIT 23 Triage routing labels · 9 Metadata labels · 6 labels have 0 open issues

Adapter Labels Work—Core Blind Spots & Bug/Improvement Drift Do Not

Engine:* is orthogonal to pillars by design (e.g., Engine: DuckDB [7] cleanly routes 5 Reliability + 2 Adoption tickets to DuckDB maintainers). Triage broke down for two structural reasons: missing core labels and post-transfer intake drift.

Per-Issue Label Coverage (n = 211)0 vs. 1 vs. 2+ labels

Excluding Engine:* & Table Format:*, 190 / 211 (90.0%) open issues have zero workstream labels—and only 2 issues (0.9%) combine two routing labels.

Open Backlog by Quarter: Labeled vs. UnlabeledClick bar to inspect

Completely unlabeled issues rose from 17.3% (24/139) pre-LF (< 2026-03-25) to 50.0% (36/72) post-LF—and Bug (51) misses #5629, #5757, #6135, and #6014 (tagged Improvement/Feature).

Before proposing any changes to our 32 repository labels, let's recognize what already works. Engine:* and Table Format: Iceberg are orthogonal to Pillars in a healthy way: Engine: DuckDB has 7 issues—5 Reliability and 2 Adoption—which is exactly right because the same adapter maintainers own both.

The two charts show what actually broke. On the left, 152 of 211 issues have zero triage routing labels—rising to 190 of 211 if an issue isn't tied to a specific SQL engine. On the right, completely unlabeled tickets jumped from 17.3 percent before the March 2026 Linux Foundation transfer to 50 percent after it. Meanwhile, filtering GitHub by Bug misses regressions like #5629 and silent data corruption like #5757 and #6135 because authors filed them as Improvement.

PROPOSED LABEL ARCHITECTURE GitHub Projects v2 = Strategic Pillar · Repo Labels = Subsystem & Risk Routing

Keep Pillars for Impact—Use 3 Targeted Repo Labels to Close the 72% Gap

Rather than inventing priority labels (P0/P1) that go stale, keep Primary & Secondary Pillar as Project board fields and make repository labels a complete map of SQLMesh's subsystems:

Action Label(s) Primary Pillars Served Cataloging Gap It Solves
Add (Risk) data-correctness Reliability (15+ unrouted today) Separates silent row/column drops (, ), SCD2 history overwrites (), & false-green audits () from loud crashes.
Add (Core) core: planner-state Reliability, Scalability, Extensibility Gives core Python snapshot/evaluator (), DAG loader (), & concurrency () a routing home; absorbs Scheduler: Built-in (1).
Add (Seams) ecosystem-integration Adoption & Extensibility Clusters manifest.json (), ADBC (), OpenMetadata (), & Ossie () instead of losing 93% of Extensibility.
Keep & Normalize 13 Engine:*, Table Format: Iceberg, Project: dbt, Project: CICD Bot, Documentation; rename area: web-ui & area: ide-lsp All 4 Pillars + Uncategorized (Tech Debt / dependencies) Preserves working adapter/surface ownership while replacing legacy Project: UI (4) & Project: VSCode Extension (6) prefixes.
Retire (4) Project: Ibis (0), Scheduler: Airflow (0), codex (0), UX (1) — Removes dead 0-issue tags and ambiguous UX (#6062 routes more clearly via Scalability + core: planner-state / area: web-ui).

This table summarizes the minimal label surgery needed to make our two-axis system work in practice—without bloating GitHub with dozens of tags or P0/P1 labels that immediately rot.

We keep Strategic Pillars as fields on a GitHub Projects v2 board, and add just three repository labels where our 211-issue audit proved the 72 percent blind spot lives: data-correctness for silent wrong data and false-passing audits, core: planner-state for the Python evaluator, loader, and state engine, and ecosystem-integration for dbt artifacts, ADBC drivers, and external catalogs.

Paired with retiring four unused or ambiguous labels and normalizing area: web-ui and area: ide-lsp, virtually every open issue gets both an obvious Pillar and a concrete subsystem label.

TEAM WORKFLOW & ALIGNMENT Consistent cataloging first · Prioritization decided together afterward

How Maintainers Apply This in 30 Seconds—and What We Decide Together

With a deterministic rubric, any two maintainers triaging a new issue land on the same Pillar + Subsystem Label—giving the team structured slices to weigh priorities from.

The 4-Step Intake Rubric (Per Issue)Deterministic Tie-Break

  • Step 1 — Broken contract? Crash, regression, race, or wrong rows → Primary: Reliability (add data-correctness if silent data/audit hazard; record migration/scale context in Secondary Pillar).
  • Step 2 — Otherwise, asymptotic growth cost? O(N²) loops, 1,000+ models, TB scans, or repo-wide boilerplate → Primary: Scalability + core: planner-state or Engine:*.
  • Step 3 — Otherwise, seam vs. built-in parity? Hook/driver/schema to avoid forking → Primary: Extensibility (ecosystem-integration); built-in dbt/auth/dialect/CLI/docs → Primary: Adoption.
  • Step 4 — Pure repo housekeeping? Contributor test-runner speedups (), driver bumps (), or code questions () → Uncategorized (Tech Debt).

4 Open Questions for Maintainer ConsensusTeam Discussion

  • 1. Scope definition: Should ongoing triage cover all 211 state:open issues, or scope to a specific Linux Foundation GitHub Project v2 column?
  • 2. Where Pillars live: Track Primary & Secondary Pillar on a GitHub Project v2 board while keeping repo labels strictly for subsystem/risk routing?
  • 3. Label set & CSV review: Adopt the 3 new labels + 4 retirements, and use Download CSV catalog (now with suggested_routing_labels) to review the 60 unlabeled issues?
  • 4. sqlglot boundary: Keep parser-rooted issues ( Cause 1, ) open here under an upstream: sqlglot tag until pinned bumps land, or track upstream?

To wrap up: instead of pretending one person can lock in a Week-1 or Month-1 sprint schedule before we've talked as a maintainer group, this final slide gives us a shared 30-second intake workflow on the left and four concrete governance questions to align on together on the right.

First, do we want our shared catalog to track all 211 open issues or a specific Linux Foundation Project board column? Second, do we agree on putting Strategic Pillars in GitHub Projects v2 while keeping repo labels focused on subsystem ownership? Third, should we adopt data-correctness, core: planner-state, and ecosystem-integration, and use the catalog CSV—which now includes a suggested routing label column—to review the 60 unlabeled tickets? And fourth, how do we want to tag upstream sqlglot parser dependencies? Let's discuss—and click into any slice live in the catalog!
